summary: Defines S/MIME version 3.2, a consistent way to send and receive secure MIME data. It provides digital signatures for authentication and integrity and encryption for confidentiality. It is on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 8551.

plainLanguage.summary: S/MIME adds three services to ordinary mail: a digital signature that shows who sent a message and that nobody changed it, encryption that keeps the text private, and compression that makes it smaller. It defines the message formats and the algorithms that every implementation must support.

questions: how to sign and encrypt email with s/mime
how do you sign and encrypt a mail message
subtitle: How a mail message is signed, encrypted and compressed using MIME and the Cryptographic Message Syntax.

tldr.problem: Mail systems need one agreed way to prove who sent a message, prove it was not altered, and keep its contents private, without inventing a new format for each application.
tldr.mechanism: S/MIME wraps the MIME body in a Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) object of type SignedData, EnvelopedData or CompressedData, and carries that object in the application/pkcs7-mime media type, or as a detached signature in a multipart/signed message.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5751 is a Proposed Standard and it obsoleted RFC 3851. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 8551.

today: RFC 5751 was a Proposed Standard published in January 2010 and it obsoleted RFC 3851. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 8551.

sections.title: What S/MIME Provides
sections.content:
S/MIME, the Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions, provides a consistent way to send and receive secure MIME data. Based on the MIME standard, it adds cryptographic security services to messaging applications: authentication, message integrity and non-repudiation of origin using digital signatures, and data confidentiality using encryption. As a supplementary service it also provides message compression.

S/MIME can be used by traditional mail user agents to add these services to mail they send and to interpret them in mail they receive, but it is not restricted to mail. It can be used with any transport mechanism that carries MIME data, such as HTTP or SIP, and it can be used in automated message transfer agents that need no human involvement, for example to sign software-generated documents or encrypt FAX messages sent over the Internet.

The specification defines how to create a MIME body part that has been cryptographically enhanced according to the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) defined in RFC 5652, which is derived from PKCS #7. It also defines the application/pkcs7-mime media type used to carry those body parts, and it discusses how to use the multipart/signed media type, in conjunction with the application/pkcs7-signature media type, to transport signed messages.

Requirements and recommendations are separated for receiving agents and sending agents. Most requirements are placed on handling incoming messages and most recommendations on creating outgoing ones, in the general spirit of being liberal in what you receive and conservative in what you send. An S/MIME agent MUST follow this document, together with the Cryptographic Message Syntax document and the algorithm documents it lists, when it creates messages.
sections.plainLanguage: S/MIME adds three things to a mail message: a signature that proves who sent it and that it was not changed, encryption that hides the text, and compression that makes it smaller. It works with any transport that carries MIME data, not only with mail.

sections.title: Required Algorithms and Content Types
sections.content:
CMS allows a wide variety of options in content, attributes and algorithm support, so this section sets a base level of interoperability that every S/MIME implementation must meet.

For the digest algorithm, sending and receiving agents MUST support SHA-256, and SHOULD- support SHA-1, where SHOULD- means the authors expect the requirement to be demoted to a MAY in a future version. Receiving agents SHOULD- support MD5, so that MD5-digested S/MIME version 2 SignedData objects can still be read.

For the signature algorithm, both sending and receiving agents MUST support RSA with SHA-256, and SHOULD+ support DSA with SHA-256 and RSASSA-PSS with SHA-256, where SHOULD+ means the authors expect the requirement to be promoted to a MUST in a future version. Support for RSA with SHA-1, DSA with SHA-1 and RSA with MD5 is downgraded to SHOULD-. For the key encryption algorithm, receiving and sending agents MUST support RSA Encryption and SHOULD+ support RSAES-OAEP. The RFC also notes that version 3.1 clients might only implement key encryption with the rsaEncryption algorithm, and that version 3 clients might only implement Diffie-Hellman.

Four CMS content types are used for S/MIME. Data identifies the inner MIME message content, and a sending agent MUST use the id-data content type identifier for it. SignedData applies a digital signature to a message, providing authentication, message integrity and non-repudiation of origin, and is also used in the degenerate case where there is no signature information, to convey certificates. EnvelopedData applies data confidentiality, and the sender needs a public key for each intended recipient. CompressedData applies compression to reduce the message size; it provides no authentication, integrity, non-repudiation or confidentiality.
sections.plainLanguage: To make different implementations work together, the RFC sets a minimum set of algorithms. SHA-256 and RSA with SHA-256 must be supported, and older algorithms are kept only so that old mail can still be read.

sections.title: How an S/MIME Message Is Built
sections.content:
An S/MIME message is a combination of MIME bodies and CMS content types. The data to be secured is always a canonical MIME entity. The MIME entity, along with other data such as certificates and algorithm identifiers, is given to CMS processing, which produces a CMS object, and the CMS object is then wrapped in MIME.

Preparing the entity follows the MIME procedure with extra steps that defend against corruptions introduced by mail transport. These steps matter most for clear-signing with the multipart/signed format, and they are recommended for enveloped messages and for signed and enveloped messages so that the message can be forwarded anywhere without modification. The entity is prepared according to local conventions, the leaf parts are converted to canonical form, and an appropriate transfer encoding is applied to the leaves.

Each MIME entity MUST be converted to a canonical form that is uniquely and unambiguously representable both where the signature is created and where it is verified, and this applies to enveloping and compressing as well as signing. For entities of major type text, both the line endings and the character set must be canonicalized: the line ending MUST be the pair of characters CR and LF, and the charset SHOULD be a registered charset.

The application/pkcs7-mime media type carries CMS content types including EnvelopedData, SignedData and CompressedData. Because these are binary, base-64 transfer encoding is appropriate in most cases, in particular with SMTP transport; the transfer encoding used depends on the transport and is not a characteristic of the media type. The Content-Type header field of all application/pkcs7-mime objects SHOULD include the optional smime-type parameter, so that a receiving agent can tell what is inside without decoding the ASN.1. The smime-type values are enveloped-data, signed-data, certs-only and compressed-data. Sending agents SHOULD also emit the optional name parameter and the optional Content-Disposition field with a filename parameter, with the extensions .p7m for SignedData and EnvelopedData, .p7c for a certificate management message, .p7z for CompressedData and .p7s for application/pkcs7-signature.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is built in three steps: put the text into a standard MIME shape, run that shape through the cryptography to make a CMS object, and put the object back into a MIME part. The smime-type parameter says which kind of object it is.

sections.title: Signed, Enveloped and Compressed Messages
sections.content:
For an enveloped-only message, the MIME entity is prepared, processed into a CMS object of type EnvelopedData, wrapped in a CMS ContentInfo object, and inserted into an application/pkcs7-mime MIME entity. The smime-type parameter is enveloped-data and the file extension is .p7m. The RFC warns that sending an enveloped message without signing it does not provide data integrity: the ciphertext can be replaced in a way that still processes correctly while changing the meaning.

For a signed-only message there are two formats: application/pkcs7-mime with SignedData, and multipart/signed. The multipart/signed form is preferred for sending, and receiving agents MUST be able to handle both. The multipart/signed form is a clear-signing format, so recipients with no S/MIME or CMS facilities can still read the message, and it keeps the rest of the MIME structure intact. It uses the multipart/signed media type with two parts: the first holds the MIME entity that is signed, and the second holds the detached signature CMS SignedData object, whose encapContentInfo eContent field is absent. That second part is an application/pkcs7-signature entity with the file extension .p7s. The multipart/signed Content-Type has two required parameters, protocol and micalg. The protocol parameter MUST be application/pkcs7-signature, with quotation marks because MIME requires the slash to be quoted. The micalg parameter names the message digest algorithm or algorithms, separated by commas when there is more than one, and allows the signature to be verified in one pass; the values are md5, sha-1, sha-224, sha-256, sha-384 and sha-512.

A compressed-only message is prepared in the same way and produces a CMS object of type CompressedData, wrapped in a ContentInfo object and inserted into an application/pkcs7-mime entity, with the smime-type compressed-data and the extension .p7z. Versions of S/MIME before 3.1 did not specify any use of CompressedData and will not recognize it.

The three formats can be nested, because each is a MIME entity that encapsulates other MIME entities, and an S/MIME implementation MUST be able to receive and process arbitrarily nested S/MIME within reasonable resource limits. The operations can be applied in any order. Signing first means the signatories are then securely obscured by the enveloping, while enveloping first means the signature is applied to the already encrypted content.
sections.plainLanguage: A signed message is usually sent in two parts: the readable text, and the signature that covers it. An encrypted message is a block of ciphertext with one copy of the content key for each recipient. The two can be combined in either order.

sections.title: Certificates and Keys
sections.content:
A receiving agent MUST provide some certificate retrieval mechanism, so that it can obtain the certificates of the recipients of digital envelopes. This specification does not cover how S/MIME agents handle certificates, only what they do once a certificate has been validated or rejected. At a minimum, for an initial deployment, a user agent could send a message to an intended recipient asking for that recipient's certificate in a signed reply, and agents SHOULD provide a way for a user to store and protect certificates for correspondents so that they can be retrieved later.

All generated key pairs MUST be generated from a good source of non-deterministic random input, and the private key MUST be protected in a secure fashion. An S/MIME user agent MUST NOT generate asymmetric keys less than 512 bits for use with the RSA or DSA signature algorithms. For signatures the RFC requires a key size of 1024 to 2048 bits, and treats sizes above 2048 bits as optional. For signature verification and for decryption, a key size of 1024 to 2048 bits is required, while smaller keys may be accepted and larger keys are optional.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a message can be encrypted, the sender needs the recipient's public key, which normally comes from a certificate. Each agent needs some way to fetch and store those certificates, and each key pair needs a secure random source and a protected private key.

sections.title: What S/MIME Does Not Solve
sections.content:
The RFC starts from the position that cryptographic algorithms will be broken or weakened over time, so implementers and users need to check that the algorithms listed continue to provide the expected level of security. It points at the Million Message Attack described in RFC 3218, the Diffie-Hellman small-subgroup attacks described in RFC 2785 and the attacks against hash algorithms described in RFC 4270 as examples of such documents.

The specification uses public key cryptography and assumes that the private key is protected so that it is not accessed or altered by unauthorized parties. The choice of 2048 bits as the RSA key size is based on the desire to provide at least 100 bits of security, and an implementation MAY support key sizes beyond those recommended.

Receiving agents that validate signatures and sending agents that encrypt messages need to be cautious about the cryptographic processing they ask for. An attacker could send certificates with very large keys, for example larger than those this specification mandates, which could swamp the processing element. Agents that use such keys without first validating the certificate to a trust anchor are advised to have some form of cryptographic resource management to prevent such attacks.

Using weak cryptography offers little actual security over sending plaintext, and weak cryptography is never recommended unless the only alternative is no cryptography. RSA and DSA keys of less than 1024 bits are now considered by many experts to be cryptographically insecure, so processing previously received mail will often mean using weak keys. An implementation that supports verification of signatures made with RSA and DSA keys of less than 1024 bits MUST warn the user.
sections.plainLanguage: Algorithms that are safe today can weaken later, so the RFC asks implementers to keep checking. It also warns that a hostile sender can send very large keys to slow a recipient down, and that keys under 1024 bits are no longer considered safe.

data.title: A clear-signed message
data.code:
Content-Type: multipart/signed;
   protocol="application/pkcs7-signature";
   micalg=sha1; boundary=boundary42

--boundary42
Content-Type: text/plain

This is a clear-signed message.

--boundary42
Content-Type: application/pkcs7-signature; name=smime.p7s
Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64
Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=smime.p7s

items.title: Authentication
items.text: The signature shows which certificate the sender used.

items.title: Message integrity
items.text: The receiver can tell that the signed content was not altered.

items.title: Non-repudiation of origin
items.text: Proof that the message came from the holder of the private key.

items.title: Data confidentiality
items.text: Encryption hides the content from anyone without the key.

items.title: Compression
items.text: Reduces the size of the message, and provides no security.
